title: Obstetrics and Gynaecology
tagline: Pregnancy and birth, complications of pregnancy, contraception, fertility and gynaecological disease
summary: Women's health from pregnancy to the menopause. The course covers maternal physiology and antenatal care, the complications of pregnancy, labour and birth, the postnatal period, early pregnancy problems, contraception and subfertility, menstrual and pelvic disorders, gynaecological cancers and screening, and the menopause.
overview: Obstetrics and gynaecology deal with pregnancy, birth and the female reproductive tract. In obstetrics there are two patients at once, normal values change, and a woman can move from well to critically ill within minutes. The course therefore starts with physiology: how pregnancy changes the circulation, kidneys, breathing and clotting, and why results must be interpreted against pregnancy ranges.

The obstetric chapters follow a pregnancy from booking to the weeks after birth: antenatal screening and risk assessment; pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, bleeding, preterm birth and fetal growth restriction; labour, fetal monitoring, operative birth and the emergencies of labour; and postpartum haemorrhage, sepsis, thromboembolism and perinatal mental health. The gynaecological chapters cover early pregnancy loss and ectopic pregnancy, contraception and subfertility, abnormal bleeding, endometriosis and polycystic ovary syndrome, the cancers of the cervix, endometrium, ovary and vulva, and the menopause.

Numbers matter throughout, and the course works through them: predictive values of screening and diagnostic tests, numbers needed to treat, hCG ratios, contraceptive failure rates, the risk of malignancy index and absolute risks of hormone therapy. Management is described as principles under current UK guidance (NICE, RCOG, FSRH and the NHS screening programmes), with WHO guidance where it differs; doses are illustrative and local guidelines apply. All cases are fictional.
outcomes: Describe the physiological changes of pregnancy and interpret routine results against pregnancy reference ranges.
Record and interpret an obstetric history, including gestational age, gravidity and parity.
Outline UK antenatal care and screening, and explain the predictive values of screening tests and the prevention of rhesus disease.
Recognise and outline the management of hypertensive disorders, gestational diabetes, antepartum haemorrhage, preterm labour and fetal growth restriction.
Explain the physiology and stages of normal labour, interpret fetal heart rate monitoring, and outline induction, operative birth and the management of labour emergencies.
Recognise postpartum haemorrhage, sepsis, thromboembolism and perinatal mental illness, and outline their management.
Assess bleeding and pain in early pregnancy using ultrasound and serum hCG, and outline the management of miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy and molar pregnancy.
Compare contraceptive methods by mechanism, effectiveness and eligibility, and outline the investigation and treatment of subfertility.
Investigate abnormal uterine bleeding and pelvic pain, and outline the management of fibroids, endometriosis, polycystic ovary syndrome and pelvic inflammatory disease.
Explain cervical screening and the presentation of gynaecological cancers, and discuss the benefits and risks of menopausal hormone therapy in absolute terms.

history.title: Transfusion for postpartum haemorrhage
history.detail: James Blundell reports in The Lancet a successful transfusion of human blood to a woman bleeding after childbirth, using his own apparatus. Transfusion would not become safe until blood groups were discovered in 1901.

history.title: Handwashing against puerperal fever
history.detail: Ignaz Semmelweis, in Vienna, requires doctors and students to wash their hands in chlorinated lime solution before examining women, and deaths from puerperal fever on his ward fall sharply. His conclusions were widely rejected during his lifetime.

history.title: Chloroform for a royal birth
history.detail: After James Young Simpson introduced chloroform for pain relief in labour in Edinburgh in 1847, John Snow gives it to Queen Victoria at the birth of Prince Leopold, making analgesia in childbirth socially acceptable.

history.title: The cervical smear
history.detail: Georgios Papanicolaou and Herbert Traut publish their monograph showing that vaginal and cervical cytology can detect cancer before symptoms, the basis of cervical screening programmes that later greatly reduced cervical cancer deaths.

history.title: Ultrasound in obstetrics
history.detail: Ian Donald, John MacVicar and Tom Brown in Glasgow publish their use of pulsed ultrasound to image abdominal masses and pregnancies, beginning the use of ultrasound for dating, growth and anomaly assessment.

history.title: The oral contraceptive pill
history.detail: Building on the work of Gregory Pincus, Min Chueh Chang and John Rock, the first combined oral contraceptive is approved for contraception in the United States, followed by the UK in 1961.

history.title: Preventing rhesus disease
history.detail: Clinical trials by Cyril Clarke and Ronald Finn in Liverpool and by Vincent Freda, John Gorman and William Pollack in New York show that anti-D immunoglobulin given to RhD-negative mothers prevents sensitisation, making haemolytic disease of the newborn largely preventable.

history.title: Antenatal corticosteroids
history.detail: Graham Liggins and Ross Howie publish a randomised trial in New Zealand showing that corticosteroids given to women before preterm birth reduce respiratory distress and death in their babies, following Liggins's 1969 observations in lambs.

history.title: Birth after in vitro fertilisation
history.detail: Louise Brown is born in Oldham after the work of Robert Edwards, Patrick Steptoe and Jean Purdy, beginning the era of assisted conception; Edwards received the Nobel Prize in 2010.

history.title: Papillomavirus and cervical cancer
history.detail: Harald zur Hausen's group isolates HPV 16 from cervical cancer tissue, followed by HPV 18 in 1984, establishing the viral cause of cervical cancer and leading to HPV testing and vaccination. Zur Hausen shared the 2008 Nobel Prize.

references.authors: F. Gary Cunningham, Kenneth J. Leveno, Jodi S. Dashe, Barbara L. Hoffman, Catherine Y. Spong and Brian M. Casey
references.note: Twenty-sixth edition. The comprehensive reference for maternal physiology, pregnancy complications and labour, from a US perspective.

references.note: Sixteenth edition. A standard reference for benign gynaecology, reproductive endocrinology, infertility and gynaecological oncology.

references.title: Antenatal care (NG201), Hypertension in pregnancy (NG133), Intrapartum care (NG235) and Menopause (NG23)
references.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
references.note: The NICE guidelines that set UK practice for the topics in this course; check the current versions online, as they are updated regularly.

references.title: Green-top Guidelines
references.authors: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
references.note: Evidence-based UK guidance on specific problems, including postpartum haemorrhage, shoulder dystocia, ectopic pregnancy, recurrent miscarriage and hyperemesis gravidarum.

references.title: UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (UKMEC)
references.authors: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare
references.note: Amended 2019. The reference for which contraceptive methods are safe for women with particular medical conditions, with FSRH guidance on individual methods.

references.title: Saving Lives, Improving Mothers' Care
references.note: The annual UK confidential enquiry into maternal deaths and morbidity; reading its case lessons is the best way to understand why the warning signs in this course matter.

references.title: WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
references.note: The international framework for antenatal care, useful for comparing UK practice with care in other settings.
